context: Bounding the in-degree of a node in the dependency graph. We convert the dependency graph G into another graph G0 where-in the in-degree of each node is bounded by 2 with in-degree of the root being 1. This is done as follows (Figure 3(a)-(b)): let T be a tree in G. T is converted into a binary tree using the standard procedure after sorting the children of node j 0 from left to right in non-decreasing order of distance from j 0 i.e., for each child k 0 (except for the nearest child) of j 0 , add an edge to its left sibling with weight 2c(k 0 , η(k 0 )) and remove the edge (k 0 , j 0 ). There is no change in the outgoing edge of the leftmost child of j 0 . Let ψ(j 0 ) be the parent of node j 0 in G0 . Its easy to see that c(j 0 , ψ(j 0 )) ≤ 2c(j 0 , η(j 0 )). Henceforth whenever we refer to distances, we mean the new edge weights. But we do not know how to do that. However, for every such cluster center j 0 , we will identify a set of centers which will be able to take care of the demand of j 0 and each one of them is within a distance of O(`)c(j 0 , ψ(j 0 )) from j 0 . We exploit the following observation to make groups of ` clusters: each cluster has facilities opened in it to an extent of at least (1 − 1/`). Hence, every collection of ` clusters, has at least ` − 1 facilities opened in it. Thus, we make groups (called meta-clusters), each consisting of ` clusters, if possible. For every tree T in G0 , MCs are formed by processing the nodes of T in a top-down greedy manner starting from the root as described in Algorithm 2. (Also see Figure 3(c)). There may be some MCs of size less than `, towards the leaves of the tree. Let Gr denote a MC with r being the root cluster of it. With a slight abuse of notation, we will use Gr to denote the collection of centers of the clusters in it as well as the set of clusters themselves. Let H(Gr ) denote the subgraph of T induced by the nodes in Gr . H(Gr ) is clearly a tree. We say that Gr is responsible for serving the demand in its clusters.
